task: SSS v7: two catalog tests of the insolation-driven deep-devolatilization (karst) model

thermal_model.description: 1-D heat equation over the 176-day solar day, 3:2 spin-orbit resonance, e=0.2056, obliquity ignored, Bond albedo 0.09, emissivity 0.95, thermal inertia 47 J m-2 K-1 s-0.5. Driven to radiative steady state by a flux-balance accelerator; deep-layer temperature = mean annual surface temperature.
thermal_model.validation: peak equilibrium T 702 K at the hot-pole equator and 570 K at the warm pole, matching published values

test_1_depth_vs_temperature.data: Blewett et al. 2016 shadow-length depths, n=2518, with pixel scale
test_1_depth_vs_temperature.prediction: diffusion-limited relief h = sqrt(2 mu D Pv f t / (R T rho)) gives d ln(h)/d(1/T) = B/2 = -4514 K for elemental sulfur
test_1_depth_vs_temperature.robustness: slope -146 to -158 K across thermal inertia 21-103; null permutation sd 54 K; attenuation would require 96.7% of modeled 1/T variance to be noise
test_1_depth_vs_temperature.verdict: REJECTED. Hollow depth is independent of mean annual temperature over 105 K, and at the actual mean annual temperatures sulfur cannot deliver the observed 20.8 m median anywhere on the planet, even at the most favorable transport parameters. Insolation alone cannot drive deep devolatilization. Depth is layer-limited, not rate-limited.

test_2_crater_size_insolation_interactio.data: 707 hollow-hosting craters from host_assignments, 511 matched into the Herrick post-flyby catalog of 16876 craters
test_2_crater_size_insolation_interactio.prediction: an impact-supplied thermal boost scaling with melt volume should let large craters host hollows at lower insolation: negative Tmean x logD interaction
test_2_crater_size_insolation_interactio.clean_design: hot-pole vs warm-pole longitude at |lat|<=60; imaging coverage tracks latitude, not longitude, so this cannot be a coverage artifact
test_2_crater_size_insolation_interactio.split_sensitivity: interaction strengthens monotonically with the size cut: -0.0058 (30 km) to -0.0214 (120 km)
test_2_crater_size_insolation_interactio.crater_size_vs_area: logD coefficient 2.909 +/- 0.123 against the 2.0 expected if hosting simply scaled with crater area; excess z=7.4
test_2_crater_size_insolation_interactio.freshness: rayed craters +6.96 +/- 4.40 K (p=0.11, wrong sign for a decaying pulse); shallow-interior craters -2.29 +/- 2.29 K (p=0.32). Null.
test_2_crater_size_insolation_interactio.verdict: SUPPORTED for crater size, NULL for crater freshness. Hollows in craters below 60 km need the hot longitudes; hollows in craters above 60 km do not. The null freshness result argues the thermal boost is not what sustains present activity.

synthesis: Insolation cannot excavate hollows at depth, so an external heat source is required, and crater size - not crater freshness - carries that signature. The absence of a freshness signal means hollow activity is decoupled in time from the thermal event, which is the collapse-doline reading: the impact-era thermal pulse creates the void volume, and collapse of that fossil void, triggered by slow present-day near-surface sublimation, produces and refreshes the landform long afterward.
caveats: Blewett shadow-length depths carry a strong pixel-scale trend (R2 0.54 between craters); all regressions control for it but the correction is not perfect.
511 of 707 hosts matched into the Herrick catalog; the unmatched 196 are mostly basins and may bias the large-D end.
The Herrick freshness flags (rayed, interior shape) are morphological classes, not ages; a proper crater-degradation chronology would be a better test.
The thermal model has no slope or aspect resolution, so wall hollows sit at temperatures the model does not resolve.

test_3_speyerer_change_character.verdict: PASSES, in the form the data can test, on a thin sample. Detectable activity on hollows is discrete, localized, and brightening, two orders of magnitude rarer than pervasive detectable change, at a rate consistent with renewing hollow surfaces within their ~10^5-yr maximum model age. The on-hollow association rests on one catalog-confirmed site (Sholem Aleichem, p = 0.04 alone) and one site the catalog does not confirm (Lermontov, 11.3 km from the nearest detection). The test is asymmetric: it cannot exclude a slow pervasive component, and it does not discriminate episodic collapse from other discrete mechanisms such as slope failure on hollow walls.
